source.title: A Deep Conditioning Treatment of Neural Networks
source.authors: Naman Agarwal; Pranjal Awasthi; Satyen Kale

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent cutoff affecting the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: Compares training and test accuracy for batch normalization, layer normalization, and normalized ReLU on CIFAR-10 networks, using accuracy curves rather than the original studies’ measures.
record.gate_note: The CIFAR-10 accuracy curves are reported in figures, with qualitative descriptions in the text. The paper also gives theoretical convergence results for square-loss training, but those do not measure the classification-error outcomes in the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The experiments benchmark NormReLU against normalization methods, changing the activation and normalization recipe together. They do not compare otherwise identical networks with and without batch normalization or test Fixup's training speed and stability. The theoretical results concern conditioning and square-loss convergence in fully connected networks, outside the specified versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record fairly summarizes the empirical conclusion: NormReLU is a viable replacement for batch or layer normalization in the tested networks, with comparable generalization and sometimes faster optimization. It omits the central theoretical conclusion that normalized activations yield conditioning improvements with depth and corresponding square-loss convergence guarantees.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares batch/layer normalization with normalized activations on CIFAR-10 and reports accuracy curves; it does not reproduce the original studies’ full model and benchmark recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported comparison varies architecture and depth, and the authors note that NormReLU required small learning rates to stabilize training while batch and layer normalization tolerated larger rates.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report faster optimization with NormReLU than batch or layer normalization in fully connected CIFAR-10 networks, using separately selected learning rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalized activations can provide a competitive alternative training recipe to batch or layer normalization.

fits_no_version.finding: NormReLU replacement gives similar ResNet test accuracy, with a slight advantage at depth 110; NormReLU and SeLU have similar training behavior.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alternative normalized activations can train the tested CIFAR-10 architectures competitively.

fits_no_version.finding: Batch and layer normalization tolerate larger learning rates than NormReLU. Appendix I.3 reports 0.01 versus 0.0009 for depth-32 fully connected BN versus NormReLU, and 0.1 versus 0.009 for ResNet-32.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning-rate sensitivity differs between the tested normalization and activation recipes; this comparison does not isolate the effect of adding batch normalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorems establish improved kernel conditioning with depth and fast square-loss convergence under normalized activations and sufficient width.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Depth can improve conditioning and gradient-descent convergence in sufficiently wide fully connected networks under the stated assumptions.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Algorithmic Learning Theory
record.problems: The relevant training results are principally shown as curves without numeric values or uncertainty estimates. The NormReLU comparisons change the activation and normalization recipe together, so they do not isolate the effect of batch normalization against an otherwise identical network without it.
record.rows_left_out: R5 is omitted because Figure 7 compares NormReLU and SeLU, not the batch/layer normalization conditions named by V6. Theoretical square-loss convergence results and test-accuracy-only comparisons do not measure the training classification behavior in the versions.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error in sufficiently large convolutional networks, including random labels, and its dependence on size, stopping and regularization.
Spurious-minimum frequency in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and the effect of one or two extra student neurons.
Depth degradation in plain batch-normalized convolutional networks versus identity shortcuts, very deep plain tanh training, and Fixup training without normalization.
Effects of activation-matched initialization on training speed and depth, including controlled orthogonal-versus-Gaussian comparisons.
Recovery, divergence and sharpness dynamics relative to a learning-rate stability threshold.
Accuracy gains and learning-rate tolerance from adding batch normalization to otherwise identical networks; Fixup matching normalized residual networks in training speed and stability.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text does not expose the plotted curve values. Section 7's approximate 10^-5 learning-rate statement differs from the explicit experimental settings in Appendix I.3. Neither the NormReLU benchmark nor its test-accuracy comparison with Fixup warrants a verdict on V6.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 classification error, corrupted or random labels, and effects of model size, early stopping, or regularization are not tested as described.
No two-layer teacher-student local-minima experiment or student-width sweep.

No comparison of plain and shortcut networks at increasing depth as described. ResNet experiments retain skip connections; the no-batch-normalization ResNet experiment uses NormReLU rather than Fixup.

No controlled comparison of activation-matched initialization schemes or orthogonal and Gaussian initialization. The Fixup comparison changes both activation and initialization and reports test accuracy.
No learning-rate stability-threshold or sharpness measurements.
The study compares batch normalization and layer normalization with NormReLU on CIFAR-10, but does not test Inception/ImageNet, VGG, or Fixup itself.
